summary: This informational memo describes CAST-128, an existing encryption algorithm with a range of key sizes, offered to meet the need for an unencumbered cipher usable in cryptographic applications and protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: CAST-128 is a symmetric encryption algorithm described for use in cryptographic applications and protocols. It supports several key sizes and uses a round-based process to transform a 64-bit block.

subtitle: An unencumbered encryption algorithm with variable key sizes and a 64-bit block.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed an encryption algorithm with a range of key sizes that could be used in different cryptographic applications and protocols.
tldr.mechanism: CAST-128 is a Feistel cipher that splits a 64-bit block into two halves and processes them through 12 or 16 rounds using subkeys, rotations and substitution boxes.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo describes the algorithm and says it is available worldwide on a royalty-free basis for commercial and non-commercial use.

facts.label: Rounds
facts.value: 12 rounds up to 80-bit keys; 16 rounds above 80 bits

today: RFC 2144 is an Informational memo that describes CAST-128. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The CAST-128 Algorithm
sections.content:
RFC 2144 describes CAST-128, a DES-like Substitution-Permutation Network (SPN) cryptosystem in the class of Feistel ciphers. The authors state that it appears to resist differential, linear and related-key cryptanalysis and has no weak or semi-weak keys.

The memo presents CAST-128 as a freely available algorithm for general-purpose use where cryptographic encryption is required. It documents the cipher, key schedule, substitution boxes and test vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC specifies how CAST-128 transforms data using a key. It presents the algorithm for cryptographic applications that need encryption.

sections.title: Blocks, Rounds and Decryption
sections.content:
CAST-128 takes a 64-bit plaintext block and a key, then divides the block into left and right 32-bit halves. Its key schedule derives pairs of subkeys for the rounds. In each round, one half is transformed using a round function and combined with the other half.

After the final round, the two halves are exchanged and joined to form the 64-bit ciphertext. Decryption uses the same algorithm but applies the subkey pairs in reverse order.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm splits each input block into two halves and processes them through rounds. Decryption follows the same steps with the round keys in reverse order.

sections.title: Round Functions and Substitution Boxes
sections.content:
Each round uses one of three function types. They combine a 32-bit data value with a masking subkey using addition, subtraction or XOR, rotate the result, then use bytes of the result to select values from substitution boxes.

CAST-128 defines eight substitution boxes. Four are used by the round functions and four are used in the key schedule. The RFC explains that the three function types rotate across the rounds and that the boxes have stated nonlinearity properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Each round mixes data with a subkey and uses lookup tables to produce a new value. The rounds use three versions of this calculation.

sections.title: Variable Key Sizes
sections.content:
CAST-128 accepts keys from 40 to 128 bits in 8-bit increments. Keys shorter than 128 bits are padded with zero bytes in the least significant positions before the key schedule is applied.

Keys of 80 bits or less use 12 rounds. Keys longer than 80 bits use all 16 rounds. The RFC notes that implementations may support a subset of the available sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: The key can have different lengths, from 40 through 128 bits in 8-bit steps. Shorter keys are padded, and the shortest sizes use fewer rounds.

sections.title: Security and Availability
sections.content:
The RFC describes CAST-128 as appearing to have strength in accordance with its key size and lists resistance properties attributed to its design. It reports encryption and decryption performance of 3.3 MBytes per second on a 150 MHz Pentium processor.

The memo states that the algorithm is available worldwide on a royalty-free basis for both commercial and non-commercial uses. It is an Informational document and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors describe the algorithm's security properties and provide test vectors for checking implementations. They state that the algorithm is royalty-free for commercial and non-commercial use.

references.text: Adams, C., "Constructing Symmetric Ciphers using the CAST Design Procedure", Designs, Codes, and Cryptography.
